Question: What's the use of async controller actions in C#/.NET?
Old_Answer: —Jan, can you explain what initiating an asynchronous operation really means? Well, it means using a controller action in C#/.NET for operations that take an unacceptably long time to complete. —Such as? Things like querying a database, reading or writing files, making network requests, or doing complex calculations or data processing. —Why do I need to async such tasks? Well, if you don’t, in other words, if they’re done synchronously, you would cause the current thread to wait until they’re finished. —Is that bad? Bad is not the right word, although it can be. I’d say wasteful. —Ok, how does it work? An async operation is initiated that consists of two steps: a thread is used to initiate the task, but because the action takes time, the thread is freed for other tasks; once the initiated task is completed, a thread is re-employed to finish the remainder of the task. See a diagram here: —That is not very clear, although I get the main idea. Could you elaborate? Sure. Let’s see a more detailed one: When the await keyword is used, it says “start this operation, and then free up the current thread to do other work instead of waiting for this operation to finish”. —What’s an example of ‘this operation’? How is ‘this operation’ done now that we freed up the thread? Won’t it need a thread to be finished? An example is fetching data from the database. Now the responsibility of the task has been passed to the database to do its job, so our application thread is available again. We free the thread, so some other tasks can use it. —Ok, why is freeing up the current thread a good thing? Well, then the server can handle a higher number of concurrent requests without exhausting the available thread pool. Particularly important in scenarios with high traffic or long-running operations. —So, it allows my application to handle more requests and do other work while waiting for the database operation to complete? Exactly. It improves the overall responsiveness and scalability of your application. —Right. Can you give me a code example? Of course: As you can see, Index is an async controller action that fetches a list of employees from a database. —I see async in its declaration on line 15. Yeah, and await on 17 calling _context.Employees.ToListAsync(), a potentially long-running operation (because it queries a database). —Ok, so what does await do? It tells the .NET runtime to “pause” the Index() method and return control to its caller. Now the current thread is freed up to do other work. —And what happens after the database operation is completed? Once the database operation is complete, the .NET runtime schedules the remainder of the Index() method to continue executing. —Correct me if I’m wrong: when the operation is complete, the .NET runtime is notified to schedule the remainder of the async method (the code after the await keyword) to run on a thread from the available thread pool. Yes. But it doesn’t have to be the same thread that was started initially. It can be any thread. —Interesting. So in your code example, what is the remainder of the async method? In our example, when the result of _context.Employees.ToListAsync() is available, it is passed along to the View() method to generate the HTTP response. —Thanks, that makes sense now. You’re welcome.

For instance, consider a scenario where your application needs to fetch data from a remote service. If you use a synchronous action, the entire application would pause, waiting for the response, which can lead to timeouts and frustrated users. However, with async actions, you can use the `async` and `await` keywords to free up the thread, allowing it to handle other incoming requests. This is particularly beneficial in high-traffic applications where scalability is crucial. Moreover, async actions can improve the overall throughput of your application, as they enable better resource utilization. It’s important to note that while async programming can introduce complexity, especially in error handling and debugging, the performance benefits often outweigh these challenges. To implement async actions, simply define your controller methods with the `async` modifier and return a `Task<IActionResult>` instead of `IActionResult`. This approach not only enhances performance but also aligns with modern development practices, making your application more robust and future-proof. In summary, async controller actions are essential for building responsive, scalable, and efficient web applications in C#/.NET.

Using WASM, websites run more complex applications, and they load faster too; we also have more options and flexibility in how we build web apps. Old_Answer: Ah, I see. You're wondering whether some can write elegant code because their minds are wired in a certain way. The so-called hereditary advantages argument. I've met a lot of very attractive people who obviously had undergone plastic surgery. They often show me the ‘before’ photos. Politely speaking, the ‘before’ photos are nothing they should hang on walls… See where I'm going? Some things are predetermined (by randomness!) and if you've been dealt a good hand, well, then don't squander it. Those of us who were not so lucky, can opt for ‘plastic surgery’. I wasn't born a genius, although if I went all the way back to 1000 years ago or so, I'd discover I'm related to some famous polymath whose contributions have changed the world. So, I can improve my mind, at least. My point is: usually, if not always, it's not possible to be so gifted as to write elegant programs with very little effort. Unlike looks, brains are more forgiving and enjoy better plasticity. This is the good news. The bad news is, not every one knows about this, and even if they did (like probably you now), their neuro-linguistic mental models (after Bandler and Grinder) and self-efficacy (after Bandura) are not enhanced enough to give them the kind of sustained motivation that is needed to improve programming elegance via practice. In other words, most people are content with writing rubbish code, even though they could change and improve. It's the same logic in other spheres of life. The principle of ‘least cognitive effort’ is being misused or rather, abused, because the person is suffering from a mental model confusion. It's like wearing a hat that makes one lazy, mediocre and happy with status quo. Achievement motivation occurs as soon as one changes one's mental models. Even seeing others adopt great mental models helps one improve. The undisputed boxing world champion Bivol said in an interview: “I want to train hard so I can carve my name in boxing history.” That sort of mental model then provides the fuel for sustained motivation to achieve his stated goal. Most people don't even know there are mental models… And that's why the average programmer writes programs that are, in polite terms, not elegant at all, and worse, doesn't care about changing or improving: ‘don't fix it if ain't broke.’ You know.
